articles.author: Matthew Hou
articles.description:
Your Dockerfile has FROM node:latest. Your docker-compose has restart: always and no health checks. Your images are 1.2GB because you're copying node_modules in the build stage.
I know this because I've reviewed hundreds of Dockerfiles in PRs, and 80% of them have the same problems. Here's the 2026 playbook.
The typical Dockerfile I review:
FROM node:20
WORKDIR /app
COPY . .
RUN npm install
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "index.js"]

Image size: 1.1GB. Includes npm, git, build tools, and your entire source code including tests and docs.
The fix:
# Build stage
FROM node:20-slim AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --only=production
COPY src/ ./src/
RUN npm run build

# Production stage
FROM gcr.io/distroless/nodejs20-debian12
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /app/dist ./dist
COPY …

articles.description:
I've been using PostgreSQL for 9 years and I keep discovering features that would have saved me weeks of application code. Here are the ones I wish I'd learned earlier — each with a real use case from production systems.
You have a users table with first_name and last_name. Every query that needs the full name does first_name || ' ' || last_name. Every. Time.
ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN full_name text 
  GENERATED ALWAYS AS (first_name || ' ' || last_name) STORED;

-- Now you can query, index, and search on full_name directly
CREATE INDEX idx_users_full_name ON users USING gin(to_tsvector('english', full_name));

Real use case: We had a products table where price_with_tax was calculated in every API response. Moving it to a generated column eliminated thousands of lines of application-lev…

A System-Oriented Approach to Scalable Hydrological Feature Engineering


Traditional watershed delineation wasn't designed for machine learning at scale. The standard approach treats each watershed as a complete, self-contained unit, which makes sense when you're studying individual rivers. But it creates real problems when you need to train models across hundreds of locations.
We ran into this on a recent flood prediction project. The study area had almost no hydrological data, no stream gauges, no riverbed surveys, nothing you'd typically use for hydraulic modeling. So we trained an LSTM model to predict discharge instead. It worked, but there was a catch: the model could only predict flow at watershed outlets. One outlet per watershed meant we didn't have enough training points.
The ob…
